opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's interesting looking back, because AlexNet came out in 2012, right around when I was an undergrad at CMU and starting to get involved in research. But in robotics, at least from where I was sitting, it didn't feel like an overnight revolution. The computer vision folks paid attention right away, since ImageNet was their benchmark. In the robotics community the center of gravity was still very much classical: state estimation, SLAM, motion planning, optimal control, and carefully engineered perception pipelines.

The Robotics Institute had this strong systems culture. You built the whole robot, you made it work in the real world, whether that was field robotics, autonomous driving, or manipulation, and you cared a lot about reliability and guarantees. Learning was definitely there. CMU had a long tradition of machine learning, and people were doing learning from demonstration, inverse optimal control, and structured prediction for perception. But it was usually one component inside a carefully designed pipeline, not the thing driving the whole system.

So there was some healthy skepticism. People would ask whether a big neural network trained on internet images would actually help a robot grasp an object in a cluttered kitchen, with all the noise, physics, and distribution shift. That wasn't an unreasonable question. The data regime for robotics is just very different.

For me, that tension was formative. I could see the vision results were real and that representations learned from data were going to matter a lot. But being at the RI also taught me that a robot has to close the loop with the physical world, and that you can't just bolt a classifier onto a robot and call it intelligent. A lot of my later interest in combining learning with structure, like planning, task abstraction, and hierarchy, came from living between those two worlds. One side said "learn everything from data," and the other said "we know a lot about how the world works, so don't throw that away."

It took a few more years, maybe until around 2015 or 2016 with deep RL and end-to-end visuomotor policies, before the robotics community as a whole really shifted. But you could feel it starting during that period.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I wasn't at CMU as a PhD student, I did my PhD at Stanford. But I did spend time around the Robotics Institute as a visiting student, and that period, roughly 2013, 2014, is really interesting to look back on, because AlexNet had already happened. It was out there. People knew about it. And yet, if you walked around the RI at that time, you wouldn't have felt like a revolution was happening.

The priorities were still very much what you might call classical robotics. There was a huge emphasis on geometry, on planning, on control theory. People were working on things like SLAM, motion planning with sampling-based methods, manipulation with very explicit models of contact and physics. The culture was, you build a model of the world, you reason about it rigorously, and you prove things about your algorithm. There was a lot of pride in that rigor.

And the vision people, the ones who were paying attention to deep learning, were sort of a parallel track. You had folks doing perception who were starting to say, okay, these convolutional networks are clearly working on ImageNet, maybe they'll work on our problems too. But I remember a real skepticism from the robotics side. The argument was basically, okay, you can classify a cat in a photo, but my robot needs to pick up an object it's never seen with a gripper that has real physical constraints, and a classifier doesn't tell me anything about forces or geometry. It was seen as a perception tool, not a robotics tool.

What I think a lot of people underestimated, and I include myself in this, is how quickly the learning paradigm would eat into the parts of the stack that everyone thought were safe. Nobody at the time thought you'd learn a controller end to end from pixels. That seemed almost silly. The whole value proposition of robotics research was that you understood the system.

So looking back, there's a bit of irony. The institution had all this incredible depth in exactly the things that would later turn out to matter for learning-based robotics, real hardware, real data collection infrastructure, people who understood why robots fail. But the framing was still, learning is a component you plug in, not the organizing principle. And I think that shift in framing, from learning as a module to learning as the backbone, that's what really took a few more years to land. It wasn't that people didn't know about AlexNet. It's that it wasn't obvious yet what AlexNet meant for robots.

Deep learning was starting to change computer vision, but it wasn’t yet the default way people approached robotics. There was still a pretty big gap between recognizing something in an image and getting a robot to act successfully in the world.
